t: Why the Gospel opens with a family tree
n: Matthew begins with forty-two generations because his first readers were Jews: a Messiah had to be a son of David and a son of Abraham, and the list proves both. Four women are named — Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, 'the wife of Uriah' — outsiders and scandal included on purpose, preparing us for a virgin birth that also looks irregular.

Matthew quotes Isaiah 7:14 from the Greek Septuagint, where the Hebrew 'young woman' had become 'virgin'. The name means 'God with us', and Matthew ends his Gospel on the same note: 'I am with you all days' (28:20).

Not kings and not three — the Gospel gives neither number nor rank; they are magoi, Persian astrologer-priests, that is, pagans. Matthew's point is that the first to worship the Jewish Messiah are Gentiles guided by the sky, while Jerusalem's king wants him dead. The gifts (gold, frankincense, myrrh) were later read as king, God, and mortal man.

John's baptism was for repentance, so John himself objects. Jesus answers that it 'fulfils all justice': he places himself among sinners from the start. The voice and the dove echo Isaiah 42 and Psalm 2 — the Servant and the King in one person.

Forty days in the desert repeats Israel's forty years, and each of Jesus' three answers is a quotation from Deuteronomy 6–8 — the lessons Israel failed in the wilderness. Bread, spectacle, and power are the shortcuts to being Messiah without the cross.

'Blessed' (beati in the Vulgate) means something like 'how fortunate' — a congratulation to exactly the people the world does not congratulate. They are not commands but a portrait of the kingdom's citizens, and of Jesus himself. The mountain setting deliberately recalls Moses at Sinai.

Jesus is about to sharpen the Law six times ('You have heard… but I say to you'). This verse guards against misreading: he is not abolishing Moses but reaching the Law's intention — anger behind murder, lust behind adultery.

'Eye for eye' was originally a limit on revenge, not a licence. Jesus removes even the limit: no retaliation, love for enemies, prayer for persecutors. 'Be perfect as your Father' is about completeness of love — the sun and rain fall on everyone.

The Latin Pater noster is the prayer the West said for fifteen centuries. Its seven petitions move from God's name, kingdom and will to our bread, forgiveness, and rescue. 'Supersubstantial bread' is Jerome's famously literal rendering of a rare Greek word others translate 'daily'.

'Whatever you would that men should do to you, do you also to them.' Hillel the Elder had taught the negative form a generation earlier; Jesus states it positively and calls it the sum of 'the law and the prophets'.

A Roman officer — an occupier and a Gentile — trusts that Jesus can heal at a word, and Jesus marvels. His sentence 'Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof' is said at every Mass before communion.

t: 'Come to me, all you that labour'
n: A 'yoke' was a rabbi's whole teaching. Jesus offers his own in place of the crushing rules of the scribes: 'my yoke is sweet and my burden light'. It is one of the few places he describes his own heart: 'meek and humble'.

The sower is the first and the key: Jesus explains it (vv. 18–23) as a parable about hearing parables. The seed is the same everywhere; the soils differ. Matthew gathers seven kingdom parables into this chapter — mustard seed, leaven, treasure, pearl, net.

At Caesarea Philippi, a pagan shrine city, Peter names Jesus 'the Christ, the Son of the living God'. Jesus renames him Petrus, 'rock', and gives him 'the keys of the kingdom'. Catholic tradition builds the papacy on this verse; it is why Peter's name appears first in every list of apostles.

Said before the crucifixion, this would have sounded like 'walk to your own execution'. The paradox that follows — lose your life to find it — is the most repeated saying of Jesus, appearing six times across the four Gospels.

Peter offers seven, a generous number. Jesus answers with a number meant to be uncountable, then tells of a servant forgiven a debt of ten thousand talents — roughly the tax revenue of a kingdom — who strangles a colleague over a hundred pence. Forgiveness received must become forgiveness given.

A trap: say yes to the tax and lose the crowd, say no and be reported to Rome. Jesus asks for the coin — they, not he, carry Caesar's image — and answers with a line that has framed every debate about church and state since.

Jesus joins two verses from the Law — Deuteronomy 6:5 (love God) and Leviticus 19:18 (love your neighbour) — and says everything else hangs on them. Neither was new; putting them together as one answer was.

Herod's Temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world; its foundation stones can still be seen. Within forty years, in AD 70, Roman legions burned it. Everything that follows in this chapter — the 'abomination of desolation', wars, false messiahs — mixes that coming catastrophe with the end of the age.

The last of Jesus' teaching before the Passion. The judgement turns not on creed but on food, drink, welcome, clothing, care and visits — and neither the saved nor the lost knew they were dealing with Christ. 'As long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me.'

At a Passover meal, whose bread and cups already carried the memory of the Exodus, Jesus attaches his own death to the bread and wine: a 'new testament' in his blood, echoing Exodus 24 and Jeremiah 31. The Eucharist begins here.

The only place the Gospels show Jesus afraid. 'Let this chalice pass from me' — the cup is an Old Testament image of God's wrath (Isaiah 51:17). The disciples, asked to watch one hour, sleep three times, a quiet echo of Peter's three denials to come.

Matthew keeps the Aramaic cry and translates it: 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' It is the first line of Psalm 21 (22 in Hebrew numbering), a psalm that begins in abandonment and ends in praise. The bystanders mishear it as a call to Elijah.

The Gospel that began 'God with us' ends 'I am with you all days'. 'All nations' overturns the earlier limit to Israel (10:5), and the threefold name — Father, Son, Holy Ghost — is the seed of the baptismal creed.

Mark is the earliest Gospel and the shortest; he has no birth story and starts with the adult Jesus at the Jordan. 'Gospel' (evangelium) was a Roman word for the good news of an emperor's victory or accession — Mark borrows it for a Galilean carpenter.

Everything Jesus preaches is summarised here: the time is fulfilled, the kingdom is near, repent and believe. 'Kingdom of God' does not mean heaven after death but God's rule arriving on earth — the thing the Lord's Prayer asks for.

The scribes are right that only God forgives sins — that is the point of the story. Jesus proves the invisible claim by a visible one: the paralytic walks. It is the first of five conflicts in Mark 2–3 that end with a plot to kill him.

Sudden storms still hit the Sea of Galilee. In the Old Testament only God commands the sea (Psalm 106 in the Vulgate; Job 38). The disciples' question — 'Who is this, that both wind and sea obey him?' — is the question the whole Gospel answers. Note the Vulgate's verse numbers run one behind modern Bibles here.

t: The woman with the flow of blood
n: Twelve years of bleeding made her ritually unclean and untouchable (Leviticus 15). She breaks the rule to touch him; instead of her uncleanness passing to Jesus, his power passes to her. He calls her 'daughter' — the only woman he addresses so.

The hinge of Mark. Peter confesses Christ and immediately rejects a suffering Christ — the same temptation the devil offered in the desert. From here the road turns toward Jerusalem, and Jesus predicts his death three times.

Moses (the Law) and Elijah (the Prophets) stand with Jesus; the cloud and voice repeat Sinai. Peter wants to build tents and stay; the voice says only 'hear him'. The Eastern Church keeps this as the image of what humanity is made for.

t: The rich young man and the camel
n: The only person in Mark whom Jesus is said to 'love' walks away sad. The camel and the needle's eye is deliberate hyperbole — there was no small gate in Jerusalem by that name; the medieval 'needle gate' explanation is a later invention. 'With God all things are possible.'

Mark's clearest statement of why Jesus dies. 'Ransom' is the price paid to free a slave; 'for many' echoes the Suffering Servant of Isaiah 53, who bears the sins of many. The Son of man comes not to be served but to serve.

Two lepta, the smallest coins in circulation. Jesus measures giving not by amount but by what is left over. Placed just after his attack on scribes who 'devour the houses of widows', the scene is also a lament.

Mark's Gospel opened calling Jesus 'Son of God'; no human being says it until here, and the one who does is a pagan executioner looking at a dead man. The Temple veil tears from the top down — God's doing — opening the Holy of Holies.

The oldest manuscripts stop at verse 8: the women flee the empty tomb and 'said nothing to any man, for they were afraid.' Verses 9–20, in the Vulgate and most Bibles, are an early summary added to round the Gospel off. Either way, the reader is left to carry the news the women could not.

Gabriel's greeting, Ave gratia plena, opens the Hail Mary. Mary's question is practical, not doubting, and her consent — 'be it done to me according to thy word' (fiat) — is the moment the Incarnation begins. Painters made this scene more often than any other in the Gospel.

Mary's song, modelled on Hannah's in 1 Samuel 2, is the Church's evening canticle. It is startlingly political: the mighty pulled from their thrones, the rich sent away empty. The Vulgate's opening word, Magnificat, gave it its name.

Luke ties the birth to Roman history — Augustus, a census, the governor Quirinius — and to David's town. 'No room in the inn' probably means the guest room of a crowded house; the manger tells us the baby lay where animals fed.

Old Simeon's prayer on seeing the child — 'Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, in peace' — is sung at Compline every night. He is the first to say the child is for Gentiles too, 'a light to the revelation of the nations'.

Reading Isaiah 61 in his home synagogue, Jesus announces the passage is fulfilled 'this day'. The crowd turns when he reminds them that Elijah and Elisha helped foreigners. Luke puts this first in the ministry as a preview of the whole story: the Gospel goes to the outsiders.

Luke's version of the Beatitudes is on a plain, not a mountain, and is blunter: not 'poor in spirit' but 'poor', and each blessing has a matching 'woe' to the rich, the full, the laughing, and the well-spoken-of.

t: The woman who washed his feet
n: A Pharisee's dinner, a woman of the city, tears and hair and ointment — a scandal in the host's eyes. Jesus' short parable of two debtors turns the room around: she loves much because she has been forgiven much. Tradition later merged her with Mary Magdalene, though Luke does not.

The Jericho road drops 3,000 feet through bandit country. A priest and a Levite pass by — perhaps fearing the corpse-uncleanness that would bar them from the Temple. The hero is a Samaritan, a member of a despised heretical people. Asked 'who is my neighbour?', Jesus answers with 'who acted as one?'

Mary sits at Jesus' feet — the posture of a disciple with a rabbi, a place women were not given. 'One thing is necessary' has been read for centuries as the contemplative life set above the active, though the story is gentler: Martha is loved, not scolded away.

Asking for the inheritance early was wishing the father dead. The father runs — undignified for an eastern patriarch — and interrupts the rehearsed apology. The story is unfinished: we never learn whether the elder brother, standing outside the party, goes in. It is addressed to the Pharisees.

The rich man has no name in the text — 'Dives' is just the Latin for 'rich'. The beggar has one. Their positions reverse after death, and the chasm cannot be crossed. The last line is a warning about the coming resurrection: 'neither will they believe, if one rise again from the dead.'

Tax collectors worked for Rome and skimmed the difference; Pharisees were the devout. The prayer of the second — 'God, be merciful to me a sinner' — became the model of all Christian prayer. 'Justified' here is the word Paul will build Romans on.

A chief publican — rich, small, and hated — climbs a sycamore to see. Jesus invites himself to dinner, and the man gives half his goods away and repays fourfold, the restitution the Law demanded of a thief. 'The Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost' sums up Luke's Gospel.

t: The agony and the sweat of blood
n: Only Luke, 'the physician', records the sweat 'as drops of blood' and the strengthening angel. Some ancient manuscripts lack the two verses; the Vulgate keeps them. It is the most human moment of the Passion.

Only Luke gives the dialogue between the two crucified criminals. The second asks only to be remembered; he receives the first explicit promise of heaven in the Gospels: 'This day thou shalt be with me in paradise.' Tradition names him Dismas.

Two disciples walking away from Jerusalem, a stranger who explains 'in all the scriptures the things that were concerning him', and recognition only 'in the breaking of the bread' — Luke's picture of how the risen Christ is met: in Scripture and Eucharist. Cleopas's companion is never named; readers have long put themselves there.

t: The Prologue: 'In the beginning was the Word'
n: John opens not in Bethlehem but before creation, echoing Genesis 1. 'Word' (Logos, Verbum) meant reason and speech to Greeks, and God's creative word to Jews. Verse 14 is the centre of Christian belief: 'the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.' This passage was read at the end of every Mass for four centuries.

The Baptist's title for Jesus gathers the Passover lamb, the daily Temple sacrifice, and Isaiah's Servant 'led as a lamb to the slaughter'. The Latin Agnus Dei is sung at every Mass. John's Gospel will time the crucifixion to the hour the Passover lambs were killed.

The first of John's seven 'signs', at a village wedding. Six stone jars for Jewish purification — about 120 gallons — become the best wine. John's readers heard the point: the old rites are being filled with something new. Mary's last recorded words: 'Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye.'

A ruler of the Jews comes by night, afraid to be seen. 'Born again' can also mean 'born from above' — Nicodemus hears the first and is baffled. Verse 16, 'God so loved the world…', is the most quoted sentence in the Bible; the passage ends on light and darkness, the theme of the whole Gospel.

A rabbi did not speak with a woman alone, and Jews did not share vessels with Samaritans; Jesus does both. She has had five husbands and comes at noon to avoid the others. To this outsider, before anyone else in John, he says plainly: 'I am he' — the Messiah. She becomes the first evangelist to her town.

After feeding five thousand, Jesus says the crowd must eat his flesh and drink his blood — language so hard that many disciples leave (v. 67 in the Vulgate). The Church has always read this as the Eucharist; John has no institution narrative at the Last Supper, and this chapter stands in its place.

'He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone.' The story is missing from the oldest Greek manuscripts and probably circulated separately before finding its home here; the Vulgate includes it, and the Church counts it as Scripture. Jesus writes on the ground — what he wrote, no one knows.

The crowd picks up stones because they have understood: 'I am' (ego sum) is the name God gave Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14). John's Gospel has seven 'I am' sayings with a predicate — bread, light, door, shepherd, resurrection, way, vine — and this one without.

Kings and God himself are shepherds in the Old Testament (Psalm 22 in the Vulgate; Ezekiel 34). The 'hireling' who flees is aimed at Israel's leaders. 'Other sheep… not of this fold' are the Gentiles. The image is the oldest in Christian art — a young shepherd with a lamb on his shoulders, in the catacombs.

Four days dead — beyond the three days in which Jewish belief held the soul might linger. 'I am the resurrection and the life' is said to Martha before the miracle. In John this sign, not the Temple cleansing, is what decides the authorities to kill Jesus (11:53).

The task of the lowest slave, done by the master at supper. Peter refuses, then asks for a whole bath. John gives no bread-and-wine at this meal; this act is his Last Supper teaching — 'I have given you an example.' The Church re-enacts it on Maundy Thursday (mandatum, 'commandment', from v. 34).
Love of neighbour was old (Leviticus 19). What is new is the measure: 'as I have loved you' — said on the night of the foot-washing and the betrayal. Mandatum novum gives Maundy Thursday its name.

t: 'I am the way, the truth, and the life'
n: The farewell discourse (chapters 14–17) is Jesus' longest speech, given at table before his arrest. 'In my Father's house there are many mansions' (mansiones, resting-places) is read at countless funerals. Thomas's blunt question gets the answer that Jesus is himself the road.

Paracletus means advocate, counsellor, one called alongside. Jesus promises 'another' — implying he was the first — who will remain, teach, and remind. This is the New Testament's fullest teaching on the Holy Spirit, and the root of the doctrine of the Trinity.

Israel was God's vine in Isaiah 5 and Psalm 79 (Vulgate); the Temple gate bore a golden vine. Jesus claims the image for himself and his disciples as the branches. 'Without me you can do nothing' — the verse Augustine leaned on against Pelagius.

Jesus' longest prayer, for his disciples and 'for them also who through their word shall believe in me' — that is, for the reader. 'That they all may be one' (ut unum sint) is the text of every prayer for Christian unity. The 'hour' he has spoken of since Cana has arrived.

Pilate's question to a prisoner who has just said he came 'to give testimony to the truth' — and he does not wait for an answer. 'My kingdom is not of this world' is the Gospel's clearest word on Christ and political power.

John's crucifixion is a coronation: no darkness, no cry of abandonment. Jesus entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple, drinks the vinegar to fulfil Psalm 68 (Vulgate), and says Consummatum est — 'it is finished', the word for a completed task or a paid bill. Then he 'delivers up' his spirit, as a king dismisses a servant.

She mistakes him for the gardener — in a garden, as Genesis began. He calls her by name; she answers 'Rabboni'. Noli me tangere ('do not touch me'; better, 'do not cling') became one of art's great subjects. She is sent to the apostles as 'apostle to the apostles'.

Thomas demands the wounds; a week later he gets them, and makes the fullest confession in any Gospel: 'My Lord and my God.' The blessing that follows is for the reader who has not seen. Verse 31 states why the book was written.

Three questions by a charcoal fire, matching Peter's three denials by another charcoal fire (18:18). The threefold charge to feed the flock is the foundation for Peter's pastoral primacy; the final words foretell his death by crucifixion in Rome.

Forty days after Easter, Jesus is taken up. The disciples are told not to stare at the sky but to be witnesses 'even to the uttermost part of the earth' — the table of contents for the book of Acts. 'This Jesus… shall so come' is the source of the creed's 'he will come again'.

Pentecost was the Jewish harvest feast, fifty days after Passover, later linked to the giving of the Law at Sinai. Wind and fire were the signs at Sinai too. The list of nations reverses Babel: every language hears one message. It is the Church's birthday.

Four marks — the apostles' teaching, fellowship, 'the breaking of bread' (the Eucharist), and prayers — plus goods held in common. Luke's portrait of the ideal church, still daily in the Temple: they did not yet think of themselves as anything but Jews.

Stephen's death copies Jesus' — 'receive my spirit', 'lay not this sin to their charge'. Watching the cloaks is 'a young man named Saul', who will become Paul. Martyr means 'witness'; Augustine said the Church owes Paul to Stephen's prayer.

t: Saul on the road to Damascus
n: The persecutor is struck down by light and a voice: 'why persecutest thou me?' — Jesus identifies himself with his followers. Blinded, led by the hand, baptised by the frightened Ananias, Saul becomes Paul (the Roman name appears at 13:9). Luke tells the story three times, so central is it to Acts.

A sheet of unclean animals and a voice: 'kill and eat.' Peter refuses three times. The vision is not really about food; it prepares him to enter the house of Cornelius, a Roman centurion, and to baptise the first Gentile family — the decision that turned a Jewish sect into a world religion.

Must Gentile converts become Jews — be circumcised, keep the Law? Peter, Paul, Barnabas and James debate it in the first church council. James's ruling asks only four abstentions. The letter's phrase 'it hath seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us' became the model for every council after.

On the Areopagus, before the philosophers, Paul quotes their own poets and preaches from an altar 'to the unknown God'. They listen until he mentions resurrection, then laugh. Only a few convert — the one time in Acts that the Gospel meets Greek philosophy head-on.

One of the most detailed sea narratives from antiquity, told by an eyewitness (the 'we' of the passage): a winter gale, fourteen days adrift, the ship run aground on Malta. Paul, a prisoner, becomes the calm centre. Acts ends with him preaching in Rome 'without prohibition'.

'The just man liveth by faith' — Habakkuk 2:4, quoted here, is the sentence Paul builds the letter on and the one that changed Luther's life. 'Justice of God' (iustitia Dei) means not God's punishment but God's saving action that puts people right.

The heart of Paul's argument: all have sinned, Jew and Greek alike; all are justified freely 'by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus'. The Reformation's 'faith alone' and the Catholic reply both start from these verses; the Council of Trent and later joint declarations argued over them for four centuries.

'By one man sin entered into this world.' Paul sets two heads of humanity side by side: Adam, through whom death came, and Christ, through whom grace abounds. Augustine read verse 12 in the Vulgate's Latin ('in whom all have sinned') and built the doctrine of original sin on it.

t: 'The good which I will, I do not'
n: Paul's anatomy of the divided self — wanting the good and doing the evil. Readers have argued whether he speaks as the unconverted man or the struggling Christian. Either way, it is the most honest page in the letters, and it ends in a cry answered by chapter 8.

The summit of Romans and the passage most read at Christian deathbeds and funerals: neither death nor life, angels nor powers, height nor depth 'shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.'

After eleven chapters of theology, 'therefore': the Christian's body becomes the sacrifice, and 'be not conformed to this world' begins the ethical half of the letter. 'Reasonable service' (rationabile obsequium) entered the Roman Mass in the words of the Canon.

'There is no power but from God' — written under Nero. The most consequential political text in the New Testament, used to defend both loyal obedience and, read with Acts 5:29 ('we ought to obey God rather than men'), its limits.

Crucifixion was the death of slaves and rebels, unmentionable in polite Roman company. Paul makes it the centre: 'unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Gentiles foolishness', but to the called 'the power of God, and the wisdom of God'.

t: The earliest account of the Last Supper
n: Written about AD 54, this is older than any Gospel — the first written record of any words of Jesus. 'I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered' is the language of tradition handed on. 'Do this for the commemoration of me' is in every Eucharistic prayer.

The Church as one body with many members — eye, hand, foot — each needed, the weakest 'more necessary'. Paul is calming a congregation that ranked its members by spiritual gifts. The image became the Catholic name for the Church itself.

'Charity' in the Douay is caritas, the Latin for the Greek agape — love that gives, not love that desires. Written to a quarrelling church, not for weddings, though it is read at most. 'Through a glass in a dark manner' became 'through a glass, darkly'.

'Christ died for our sins… was buried… rose again the third day… was seen by Cephas.' Paul quotes a formula he himself received, within a few years of the crucifixion. Five hundred witnesses 'of whom many remain until this present' is an invitation to check. The chapter goes on to argue that without the resurrection the faith is empty.

'We shall all indeed rise again' — the Vulgate's rendering, famously different from the Greek, which says 'we shall not all sleep'. The trumpet, the change 'in the twinkling of an eye', and the taunt to death (from Hosea 13) close Paul's longest argument, and Handel's Messiah.

What it was — illness, eye trouble, an enemy — Paul never says, and every generation guesses. He asked three times for it to go; the answer was 'My grace is sufficient for thee; for power is made perfect in infirmity.' Weakness as the place of God's strength is the theme of the whole letter.

The one recorded quarrel between apostles: Peter had eaten with Gentiles, then withdrew when men from James arrived. Paul rebuked him 'to his face'. From this comes the letter's thesis: a man is not justified by the works of the law but by faith in Christ. 'I live, now not I; but Christ liveth in me.'

Probably an early baptismal formula: in Christ the three great divisions of the ancient world — race, class, sex — no longer determine standing before God. The verse has been quoted in every Christian argument for equality since.

Set against the 'works of the flesh' just listed. The Vulgate counts twelve fruits (the Greek has nine): charity, joy, peace, patience, benignity, goodness, longanimity, mildness, faith, modesty, continency, chastity — the list Catholic catechisms still teach.

t: 'By grace you are saved through faith'
n: Grace is God's gift, faith the open hand, works the result — 'created in Christ Jesus in good works'. Paul's most compact statement of salvation, and the verse the Reformers set beside Romans 3.

The household code of the ancient world, rewritten: it opens with mutual submission 'in the fear of Christ', and asks of husbands not authority but a love that dies for the other. 'This is a great sacrament' (sacramentum, translating mysterion) is why the Latin Church counts marriage among the seven sacraments.

Written, tradition says, from a Roman prison, with a soldier at hand. Each piece of kit is a virtue: truth, justice, peace, faith, salvation, the word of God. The enemy is not 'flesh and blood' but spiritual powers — the passage behind every 'spiritual warfare' in later Christianity.

Probably a hymn older than the letter: Christ, in the form of God, 'emptied himself' (exinanivit; Greek kenosis), took the form of a slave, obeyed to the cross, and was exalted so that 'every knee should bow'. The last line borrows from Isaiah 45, where every knee bows to God alone.
Gaudete — the Latin first word gives the third Sunday of Advent its name. Written by a man in chains awaiting a verdict. 'The peace of God, which surpasseth all understanding' closes many services.

A second Christ hymn: the firstborn of all creation, in whom all things were made and 'hold together', the head of the body, the firstborn from the dead. The New Testament's highest statement of Christ's role in creation, later a battleground in the Arian controversy over 'firstborn'.

The oldest book of the New Testament (about AD 50) answers a real worry: members had died before Christ's return. Paul's picture (verses 12–17 in the Vulgate's numbering) — the trumpet, the dead rising first, the living 'taken up' to meet the Lord in the air — is the source of the word 'rapture' (from the Vulgate's rapiemur).

The earliest job description for church office: a bishop (episcopus, 'overseer') must be sober, hospitable, a teacher, married once, ruling his own house well. Deacons follow. Church structure is already visible a generation after Jesus.

Divinitus inspirata — the phrase behind the doctrine of inspiration. 'Scripture' here means the Old Testament, the only Bible the Church yet had; the sentence would later be applied to the letter that contains it.
Paul's farewell, written from his last Roman prison: the race run, the faith kept, the crown waiting. Tradition places his beheading on the Ostian Way under Nero, around AD 67.

One of the most elegant sentences in Greek literature opens Hebrews: God spoke in fragments through prophets, and finally in a Son. Nobody knows who wrote it — 'God knows', said Origen. The Vulgate places it after Paul's letters, where it has stood ever since.

'The substance of things to be hoped for, the evidence of things that appear not.' The chapter then calls the roll of the Old Testament — Abel, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Rahab — as a 'cloud of witnesses' (12:1) to those under persecution.

The sentence that looks like a contradiction of Paul, and troubled Luther enough to call the letter 'an epistle of straw'. James is attacking a faith that is words only; Paul attacked works done to earn standing. Both cite Abraham; both would agree that real faith acts.

Titles Exodus 19 gave to Israel at Sinai, now given to Gentile converts in Asia Minor. The 'priesthood of all believers' is grounded here — and, in Catholic reading, so is the dignity of every baptised person.

t: Christ 'preached to the spirits in prison'
n: The most mysterious verse in the letter, and the scriptural root of the creed's 'he descended into hell' — the harrowing of hell in medieval art, where Christ pulls Adam and Eve from the tomb. Noah's ark, 'wherein a few, that is, eight souls, were saved by water', is a figure of baptism.

Deus caritas est — the only time the Bible defines God with a noun. 'We love, because he first loved us.' The letter's circling repetitions are its method: the same three notes — light, love, life — returned to until they are learned.

Exiled on a rocky island in the Aegean, 'on the Lord's day', John sees the risen Christ among seven lampstands — the seven churches of Asia to whom the next two chapters are addressed. 'I am Alpha and Omega' frames the whole book (1:8, 22:13).

The Lion of Judah is announced; what John sees is a Lamb 'as it were slain' — the book's central image, used twenty-eight times. Only the crucified one can open the sealed scroll of history. The 'new canticle' is one of the hymns that make Revelation the most liturgical book in the Bible.

White, red, black and pale: conquest, war, famine and death, released as the first four seals open. Dürer's woodcut fixed the image forever. Revelation was written under Roman pressure, and its 'Babylon' is Rome; the horsemen are the empire's own gifts to its provinces.

t: The woman clothed with the sun
n: A woman crowned with twelve stars gives birth while a dragon waits to devour the child. She is Israel, the Church, and — in Catholic reading — Mary; the image is behind the Virgin of Guadalupe and every 'star-crowned' Madonna. The child is 'taken up to God', the Ascension in one line.

t: 'A new heaven and a new earth'
n: Not the faithful going up to heaven but heaven coming down: the New Jerusalem 'as a bride adorned for her husband'. God 'shall wipe away all tears… and death shall be no more.' The Bible ends where Genesis began, with God dwelling among his people in a garden-city.

The last prayer in the Bible — Veni, Domine Iesu — answering the promise 'Surely I come quickly'. The bright morning star, the bride and the Spirit saying 'come', water of life freely given: the final page returns to Eden's river and tree.
